paras: The threatened lynching of fire suspects at Russellville, Indiana, followed an incendiary fire on the night of Wednesday, January 19, 1881, that burned the town's entire business district. The men accused of setting the fire, called "fire bugs," were captured and, according to a telegraph brief, "narrowly escaped lynching." The episode is known from a single sentence in the Omaha Daily Bee, which gave no names, numbers, or race for the accused.

The fire was described as "incendiary," and it destroyed "the entire business portion" of Russellville on Wednesday night. Those blamed for it were taken soon afterward, though the brief does not say who captured them or whether officers were involved. The report states only that the captured men came close to being lynched; it names no mob, gives no crowd size, and does not say where the threat occurred or how it was averted.
No report of charges, a trial, or any further action against the accused appears in the coverage.

The Omaha Daily Bee printed the item on January 21, 1881, without a headline, in a front-page column of one-line telegraph briefs between a Maine murder verdict and a Chicago printers' dispute. It used the slang term "fire bugs" for the accused and added no comment on the near-lynching. No Indiana paper's account or other wire copy of the story was found, and the brief does not mention race, so it does not show whether the accused were Black.
